translations.title: Naming the Moves
translations.explanation: Naming the Moves is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Rigid Transformations and Congruence”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:8.G.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Verify experimentally the properties of rotations, reflections, and translations: a. Lines are taken to lines, and line segments to line segments of the same length. b. Angles are taken to angles of the same measure. c. Parallel lines are taken to parallel lines. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Naming the Moves. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 3 and 7 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 3 × 7 = 21 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 5 and 3 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 5 × 3 = 15 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 3 and 7. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 21. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 5 and 3. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 15. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Naming the Moves. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Naming the Moves. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Meet Slope
translations.explanation: Meet Slope is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Dilations, Similarity, and Introducing Slope”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:8.EE.B.6. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use similar triangles to explain why the slope m is the same between any two distinct points on a non-vertical line in the coordinate plane; derive the equation y = mx for a line through the origin and the equation y = mx + b for a line intercepting the vertical axis at b. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Meet Slope. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 3x + 8 = 32. Subtract 8 and divide by 3; the solution is x = 8. Example 2: Solve 4x + 5 = 29. Subtract 5 and divide by 4; the solution is x = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 8 from both sides to get 3x = 24. Step 2: divide both sides by 3. Step 3: x=8. Step 4: substitute: 3(8)+8=32, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 5 from both sides to get 4x = 24. Step 2: divide both sides by 4. Step 3: x=6. Step 4: substitute: 4(6)+5=29, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Meet Slope. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Meet Slope. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 9 and 4. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 36. translations.title: Writing Systems of Equations
translations.explanation: Writing Systems of Equations is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Linear Equations and Linear Systems”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:8.EE.C.8. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Analyze and solve pairs of simultaneous linear equations. a. Understand that solutions to a system of two linear equations in two variables correspond to points of intersection of their graphs, because points of intersection satisfy both equations simultaneously. b. Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically, and estimate solutions by graphing the equations. Solve simple cases by inspection. For example, 3x + 2y = 5 and 3x + 2y = 6 have no solution because 3x + 2y cannot simultaneously be 5 and 6. c. Solve real-world and mathematical problems leading to two linear equations in two variables. For example, given coordinates for two pairs of points, determine whether the line through the first pair of points intersects the line through the second pair. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Writing Systems of Equations. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 4x + 8 = 20. Subtract 8 and divide by 4; the solution is x = 3. Example 2: Solve 3x + 3 = 24. Subtract 3 and divide by 3; the solution is x = 7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 8 from both sides to get 4x = 12. Step 2: divide both sides by 4. Step 3: x=3. Step 4: substitute: 4(3)+8=20, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 3 from both sides to get 3x = 21. Step 2: divide both sides by 3. Step 3: x=7. Step 4: substitute: 3(7)+3=24, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Writing Systems of Equations. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Writing Systems of Equations. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

translations.title: Inputs and Outputs
translations.explanation: Inputs and Outputs is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Functions and Volume”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:8.F.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output. The graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs consisting of an input and the corresponding output.1 Instructional focus: Students view a function as a rule assigning exactly one output to each allowed input and connect tables, graphs, equations, and verbal descriptions of the same relationship. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Inputs and Outputs. A function has one output for each input in its domain. Rate of change describes how output changes with input; an initial value describes the output at a chosen starting input. Different representations should agree on corresponding input-output pairs.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For f(x) = 2x + 2, f(4) = 2(4) + 2 = 10. The rate of change is 2 and the output at x=0 is 2. Example 2: For f(x) = 4x + 4, f(6) = 4(6) + 4 = 28. The rate of change is 4 and the output at x=0 is 4.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify input x=4. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=2x+2. Step 3: multiply 2×4=8. Step 4: add 2 to obtain 10. Step 5: interpret slope 2 and initial value 2 with the problem units. Step 1: identify input x=6. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=4x+4. Step 3: multiply 4×6=24. Step 4: add 4 to obtain 28. Step 5: interpret slope 4 and initial value 4 with the problem units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Inputs and Outputs. Do not confuse a steep graph with a large y-intercept. Check the scale before comparing rates. A vertical line generally cannot represent y as a function of x because one x-value would have more than one output.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Inputs and Outputs. Identify inputs and outputs, connect the representations, compute or interpret the rate and initial value when relevant, and verify that the function rule is consistent.

translations.title: Scaling One Dimension
translations.explanation: Scaling One Dimension is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Functions and Volume”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:8.F.A.1, CCSS:8.G.C.9. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output. The graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs consisting of an input and the corresponding output.1 Know the formulas for the volumes of cones, cylinders, and spheres and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems. Instructional focus: Students view a function as a rule assigning exactly one output to each allowed input and connect tables, graphs, equations, and verbal descriptions of the same relationship. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Scaling One Dimension. A function has one output for each input in its domain. Rate of change describes how output changes with input; an initial value describes the output at a chosen starting input. Different representations should agree on corresponding input-output pairs.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For f(x) = 4x + 6, f(4) = 4(4) + 6 = 22. The rate of change is 4 and the output at x=0 is 6. Example 2: For f(x) = 5x + 1, f(2) = 5(2) + 1 = 11. The rate of change is 5 and the output at x=0 is 1.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify input x=4. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=4x+6. Step 3: multiply 4×4=16. Step 4: add 6 to obtain 22. Step 5: interpret slope 4 and initial value 6 with the problem units. Step 1: identify input x=2. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=5x+1. Step 3: multiply 5×2=10. Step 4: add 1 to obtain 11. Step 5: interpret slope 5 and initial value 1 with the problem units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Scaling One Dimension. Do not confuse a steep graph with a large y-intercept. Check the scale before comparing rates. A vertical line generally cannot represent y as a function of x because one x-value would have more than one output.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Scaling One Dimension. Identify inputs and outputs, connect the representations, compute or interpret the rate and initial value when relevant, and verify that the function rule is consistent.

translations.title: Multiplying Powers of Ten
translations.explanation: Multiplying Powers of Ten is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Exponents and Scientific Notation”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:8.EE.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Know and apply the properties of integer exponents to generate equivalent numerical expressions. For example, 32 × 3–5 = 3–3 = 1/33 = 1/27. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Multiplying Powers of Ten. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 2x + 4 = 14. Subtract 4 and divide by 2; the solution is x = 5. Example 2: Solve 4x + 2 = 34. Subtract 2 and divide by 4; the solution is x = 8.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 4 from both sides to get 2x = 10. Step 2: divide both sides by 2. Step 3: x=5. Step 4: substitute: 2(5)+4=14, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 2 from both sides to get 4x = 32. Step 2: divide both sides by 4. Step 3: x=8. Step 4: substitute: 4(8)+2=34, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Multiplying Powers of Ten. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Multiplying Powers of Ten. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use numbers expressed in the form of a single digit times an integer power of 10 to estimate very large or very small quantities, and to express how many times as much one is than the other. For example, estimate the population of the United States as 3 × 108 and the population of the world as 7 × 109, and determine that the world population is more than 20 times larger. Perform operations with numbers expressed in scientific notation, including problems where both decimal and scientific notation are used. Use scientific notation and choose units of appropriate size for measurements of very large or very small quantities (e.g., use millimeters per year for seafloor spreading). Interpret scientific notation that has been generated by technology. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Applications of Arithmetic with Powers of 10. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 6x + 1 = 37. Subtract 1 and divide by 6; the solution is x = 6. Example 2: Solve 5x + 4 = 14. Subtract 4 and divide by 5; the solution is x = 2.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 1 from both sides to get 6x = 36. Step 2: divide both sides by 6. Step 3: x=6. Step 4: substitute: 6(6)+1=37, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 4 from both sides to get 5x = 10. Step 2: divide both sides by 5. Step 3: x=2. Step 4: substitute: 5(2)+4=14, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Applications of Arithmetic with Powers of 10. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Applications of Arithmetic with Powers of 10. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

translations.title: The Areas of Squares and Their Side Lengths
translations.explanation: The Areas of Squares and Their Side Lengths is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Pythagorean Theorem and Irrational Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:8.NS.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use rational approximations of irrational numbers to compare the size of irrational numbers, locate them approximately on a number line diagram, and estimate the value of expressions (e.g., π2). For example, by truncating the decimal expansion of √2, show that √2 is between 1 and 2, then between 1.4 and 1.5, and explain how to continue on to get better approximations. Instructional focus: Students extend arithmetic to signed, rational, and irrational numbers and reason about magnitude, order, opposites, absolute value, and operations on the number line. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: The Areas of Squares and Their Side Lengths. Position on the number line determines order. Opposites are the same distance from zero on different sides. Absolute value is distance from zero. Operation rules must be connected to direction, magnitude, or properties rather than memorized without meaning.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Start at -6 on the number line and add 6. Moving 6 units to the right lands at 0, so -6 + 6 = 0. The absolute value |-6| = 6. Example 2: Start at -6 on the number line and add 5. Moving 5 units to the right lands at -1, so -6 + 5 = -1. The absolute value |-6| = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: locate -6. Step 2: addition of positive 6 means move right 6 units. Step 3: arrive at 0. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-6|=6 records distance from zero, not the sign. Step 1: locate -6. Step 2: addition of positive 5 means move right 5 units. Step 3: arrive at -1. translations.title: Decimal Representations of Rational Numbers

Opposites are the same distance from zero on different sides. Absolute value is distance from zero. Operation rules must be connected to direction, magnitude, or properties rather than memorized without meaning.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Start at -9 on the number line and add 7. Moving 7 units to the right lands at -2, so -9 + 7 = -2. The absolute value |-9| = 9. Example 2: Start at -8 on the number line and add 5. Moving 5 units to the right lands at -3, so -8 + 5 = -3. The absolute value |-8| = 8.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: locate -9. Step 2: addition of positive 7 means move right 7 units. Step 3: arrive at -2. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-9|=9 records distance from zero, not the sign. Step 1: locate -8. Step 2: addition of positive 5 means move right 5 units. Step 3: arrive at -3. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-8|=8 records distance from zero, not the sign.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Decimal Representations of Rational Numbers. Do not confuse a negative sign with an instruction to subtract. translations.title: When Is the Same Size Not the Same Size?
translations.explanation: When Is the Same Size Not the Same Size? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Pythagorean Theorem and Irrational Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:8.G.B.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to determine unknown side lengths in right triangles in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: When Is the Same Size Not the Same Size?. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 7 and 3 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 7 × 3 = 21 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 6 and 3 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 6 × 3 = 18 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 7 and 3. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 21. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 6 and 3. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 18. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: When Is the Same Size Not the Same Size?. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: When Is the Same Size Not the Same Size?. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: What Influences Temperature?
translations.explanation: What Influences Temperature? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:8.F.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output. The graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs consisting of an input and the corresponding output.1 Instructional focus: Students view a function as a rule assigning exactly one output to each allowed input and connect tables, graphs, equations, and verbal descriptions of the same relationship. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: What Influences Temperature?. A function has one output for each input in its domain. Rate of change describes how output changes with input; an initial value describes the output at a chosen starting input. Different representations should agree on corresponding input-output pairs.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For f(x) = 2x + 7, f(4) = 2(4) + 7 = 15. The rate of change is 2 and the output at x=0 is 7. Example 2: For f(x) = 5x + 5, f(5) = 5(5) + 5 = 30. The rate of change is 5 and the output at x=0 is 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify input x=4. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=2x+7. Step 3: multiply 2×4=8. Step 4: add 7 to obtain 15. Step 5: interpret slope 2 and initial value 7 with the problem units. Step 1: identify input x=5. Step 2: substitute into f(x)=5x+5. Step 3: multiply 5×5=25. Step 4: add 5 to obtain 30. Step 5: interpret slope 5 and initial value 5 with the problem units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: What Influences Temperature?. Do not confuse a steep graph with a large y-intercept. Check the scale before comparing rates. A vertical line generally cannot represent y as a function of x because one x-value would have more than one output.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: What Influences Temperature?. Identify inputs and outputs, connect the representations, compute or interpret the rate and initial value when relevant, and verify that the function rule is consistent.

Tempo zmian opisuje zmianę wartości funkcji względem argumentu, a wartość początkowa opisuje punkt startowy. Różne reprezentacje powinny zgadzać się dla tych samych par argument-wartość.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Dla f(x) = 2x + 7, f(4) = 2(4) + 7 = 15. Tempo zmian wynosi 2, a wartość dla x=0 wynosi 7. Przykład 2: Dla f(x) = 5x + 5, f(5) = 5(5) + 5 = 30. Tempo zmian wynosi 5, a wartość dla x=0 wynosi 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: argument to x=4. Krok 2: podstaw do f(x)=2x+7. Krok 3: 2×4=8. Krok 4: dodaj 7 i otrzymaj 15. Krok 5: zinterpretuj nachylenie 2 i wartość początkową 7 z jednostkami zadania. Krok 1: argument to x=5. Krok 2: podstaw do f(x)=5x+5. Krok 3: 5×5=25. Krok 4: dodaj 5 i otrzymaj 30. Krok 5: zinterpretuj nachylenie 5 i wartość początkową 5 z jednostkami zadania.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Funkcje — What Influences Temperature?. Nie myl dużego nachylenia wykresu z dużym wyrazem wolnym. Przed porównaniem tempa zmian sprawdź skalę osi. Pionowa prosta zwykle nie przedstawia y jako funkcji x, ponieważ jednemu x odpowiadałoby wiele wartości y.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Funkcje — What Influences Temperature?. Określ argumenty i wartości, połącz różne reprezentacje, oblicz lub zinterpretuj tempo zmian i wartość początkową oraz sprawdź spójność reguły funkcji.
